title: Why Students Don't Participate In Discussions And What To Do About It s-and-what-to-do-about-it/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin challenges the conventional wisdom of pressuring reluctant students to participate through pep talks or spotlighting their contributions, arguing both tactics backfire by increasing self-consciousness and discomfort. He lays out a three-step alternative: providing explicit tools for how to participate, such as modeling how to agree, disagree, or build on a peer's idea; keeping the focus on the topic rather than the individual speaker, so no student feels singled out; and moving on quickly once a student finishes speaking, giving them a private, unspotlighted moment of success. The goal, he explains, is to create a "true safe space" where the emphasis is on removing judgment of performance rather than protecting students from disagreement — since respectful disagreement is healthy and rarely the actual reason students hold back. Linsin frames this as pulling students toward participation through psychological safety rather than pushing them with pressure or praise.
points: Direct pep talks and encouragement about participating tend to backfire by increasing a reluctant student's self-consciousness.
Students need explicit modeling of discussion skills — how to agree, disagree, or build on an idea — not just encouragement to speak up.
Keeping discussion focus on the topic, not the individual speaker, removes the spotlight that makes hesitant students hold back.
Moving on quickly after a student speaks, without lingering praise, lets them privately experience success without added pressure.
A genuine safe space is defined by removing judgment of performance, not by shielding students from respectful disagreement.
quotes: It’s a mistake because the added pressure will cause them to sink deeper in their seats (hide) or volunteer through clenched teeth (against their will).
To get everyone in your class involved, even the most reluctant students, they have to want to participate. It must be of their own volition. Therefore, you must pull, not push.
It highlights their discomfort in front of the class and labels them as shy, aloof, or awkward, which reinforces how they already feel.
They need you to model for them how to successfully take part in a discussion.
The focus of class discussions should be on the topic at hand, not individual speakers. In fact, you must behave as if you don’t give a whit who is doing the talking.
The key to getting students to participate is to make them feel safe by removing any judgment of their performance.
Your classroom should never be safe from differing ideas and opinions. Rather, it should be safe to share them.
